title: Task-Optimized Convolutional Recurrent Networks Align with Tactile Process

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states that “specialized insect hairs respond to wind stimuli” and cites Sterbing-D’Angelo et al. [2011]. The cited reference is titled “Bat wing sensors support flight control” and concerns bat-wing mechanosensors, not insect hairs. This is a direct misattribution.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, paragraph on robotic whisker sensors
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The claim that robotic whisker sensors cannot discriminate simultaneous airflow, contact, and inertia is cited to Simon et al. [2023]. The listed paper is “FlowDrone: Wind estimation and gust rejection on UAVs using fast-response hot-wire flow sensors,” not a study of whisker sensors or of separating contact, inertia, and airflow signals.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, paragraph on magnetic tactile sensors
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper cites Bhirangi et al. [2024b] for the claim that magnetic tactile sensors have low spatial resolution and are susceptible to electromagnetic interference. But the bibliography identifies Bhirangi et al. [2024b] as “Hierarchical state space models for continuous sequence-to-sequence modeling,” which is unrelated to magnetic tactile sensors. The citation cannot support the stated claim.

The authors state that active whisking was simulated using “a real recorded whisking trajectory [Bresee et al., 2023].” The cited Bresee et al. paper is “Comparative morphology of the whiskers and faces of mice ... and rats,” a morphology study. Its cited title does not support attribution of a recorded whisking trajectory to that source.

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods, Encoder-Attender-Decoder temporal model search parameterization
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The methodological rationale incorrectly characterizes Mamba as an attention-like method that “independently weight[s] each timestep.” Mamba is a selective state-space model computed by a recurrent/scan-style state update, not attention with independent timestep weighting. This matters because the claimed encoder-versus-attender division is justified using a false description of the compared architecture.

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods and Results, neural evaluation / Figure 4
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Neural alignment is evaluated on only six experimental conditions (convex/concave × three distances), as explicitly stated and shown in Figure 4 and Figure A3. An RSA over six conditions contains only 15 off-diagonal RDM entries. The study nevertheless selects the maximum score across layers and compares many architectures, losses, and training configurations on this same tiny stimulus set, without a held-out neural stimulus set or correction for layer/model selection. This makes the reported maxima and claims of ceiling saturation highly vulnerable to selection inflation and does not support the claimed general neural generalization.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, “ConvRNN Encoders Saturate Explainable Neural Variance in Rodent Somatosensory Cortex”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper claims that the best models “saturated all of the held-out explainable neural variance—without fitting any additional parameters.” However, the method explicitly obtains each model score by taking “the maximum, across all layers” of neural RSA. Selecting the best layer against the neural data is a form of neural-data-driven model selection, and no held-out neural conditions are described. Thus “held-out explainable variance” and “without fitting” are misleading descriptions of the actual evaluation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 4 caption versus Appendix A4, “Inter-Animal Consistency”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Figure 4 states that the maximum pairwise animal-to-animal score is 0.34. Appendix A4 instead states that the mean pooled animal score is 0.175 and the “maximum score” is 1.34. These cannot be presented as the same inter-animal benchmark without an explicit distinction in metric, normalization, or population definition. The paper makes no such distinction, while using the benchmark to support central ceiling and Turing-test claims.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, “ConvRNN Encoders Saturate Explainable Neural Variance”; Figure 4
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The manuscript treats an inter-animal maximum of 0.34 in Figure 4 as a meaningful ceiling/baseline while reporting model neural-fit values near 0.96 in Table 7 and claiming that models “saturate” explainable variance. If 0.34 is the stated maximum inter-animal reliability benchmark, a model score near 0.96 is not saturation of that benchmark but a nearly threefold exceedance. Appendix A4's incompatible 1.34 number further prevents interpretation. The ceiling claim requires correction and a coherent reliability calculation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, statement that all trained EAD models outperform raw inputs; Table 7
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Results state that raw model input has neural correlation 0.46 and that “All trained EAD models outperformed raw sensor inputs in neural alignment.” Table 7 reports a trained “Inter+SimCLR with Temporal Masking” neural fit of 0.42, below 0.46. Under the paper's own reported metric, this trained model does not outperform the raw-input baseline.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, tactile categorization comparison; Figure 3 and Discussion
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Figure 3 says that models with S4 encoders are excluded because “training losses explode before the first epoch is finished.” Nevertheless, the Abstract, Introduction, Results, and Discussion repeatedly conclude that ConvRNNs outperform S4/state-space architectures for tactile categorization and neural alignment. A method that was not successfully trained and is excluded from the task-performance figure is not a valid performance baseline for a claim of architectural superiority without a stabilized implementation, fair tuning, or a clearly limited claim that the tested S4 setup was unstable.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 5a legend and Appendix Figure A1 legend
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Methods say SSL experiments use SimCLR, SimSiam, and autoencoding. Figure 5a instead labels SSL losses “SimCLR,” “SwAV,” and “AE”; SwAV is never introduced, trained, or configured. Appendix Figure A1 additionally lists losses “simsiam” and “vicreg,” and attenders “cnn” and “llama,” none of which are described as evaluated EAD choices in the Methods or Results. These inconsistent legends make it impossible to identify which models generated the plotted results and suggest mislabeled or imported figures.

Table 6 says that for each of the six stimuli the authors train on the other five and test on the one held-out stimulus. With one prediction per held-out stimulus, a single leave-one-condition-out accuracy over six conditions must be an integer multiple of 1/6 (for example, 0.50, 0.67, or 0.83). Reported model values such as 0.56, 0.58, 0.54, 0.43, 0.48, 0.52, and 0.57 cannot arise from the described six-test procedure unless results were averaged over unreported repetitions, samples, folds, or seeds. The protocol and reported numbers are therefore inconsistent.

The text says temporal masking improved top-5 task performance by “~5%.” Table 7 reports 0.15 to 0.18 for Inter+SimCLR and 0.23 to 0.28 for Resnet+Mamba+SimCLR. These are 3 and 5 percentage-point increases, respectively, but approximately 20% and 22% relative increases. Calling both “~5%” without specifying percentage points misstates the numerical effect; moreover, the same masking substantially reduces Inter+SimCLR neural fit from 0.96 to 0.42.
